title: Adiós a la vergüenza de pedir las sobras de la comida - AECOC
description: Arranca una campaña en Cataluña para que restaurantes den una bolsa a los clientes para llevarse la comida sobrante para acabar con el desperdicio de comida
text:
Adiós a la vergüenza de pedir las sobras de la comida
Arranca una campaña en Cataluña para que restaurantes den una bolsa a los clientes para llevarse la comida sobrante
Un paso más para acabar con el desperdicio de comida. Un grupo de entidades catalanas ha arrancado esta semana la campaña «Remenja’mmm» («Recómeme»), a la que se han adherido de momento nueve restaurantes de Barcelona, que repartirán bolsas de papel entre los comensales para que se puedan llevar la comida sobrante y reducir el despilfarro alimentario.
La campaña, que también pretende sensibilizar a los usuarios y a la industria de la restauración y hostelería, ha sido organizada conjuntamente por las entidades Nutrición Sin Fronteras, la Fundación Prevención de Residuos y Consumo (Rezero), Banco de Recursos y el grupo GSR de producciones de gastronomía, para recuperar el excedente que se genera por parte de los comensales.
Se estima que en Cataluña cada día se tiran 720.000 kilos de comida a la basura, y de las 262.471 toneladas que se despilfarran anualmente, un 16 % proviene del sector de la restauración.
La coordinadora de Rezero, Marta Beltran, ha explicado que su misión es ofrecer a los restaurantes «una solución práctica para el excedente», la bolsa «doggy bag», para que los clientes puedan llevarse a casa la comida que no se han podido terminar en los restaurantes, y así normalizar esta práctica, que ya es común en otros países.
Visibilizar el despilfarro
Otros propósitos de las entidades son hacer visible la problemática del despilfarro, compartir las oportunidades de prevención, difundir buenas prácticas e implicar a las administraciones públicas y a los sectores involucrados.
La coordinadora de la Fundación Banco de Recursos, Mariona Ortiz, ha explicado que adherirse a la iniciativa es gratuito y, tras hacerlo, los restaurantes recibirán las bolsas, un adhesivo acreditativo y material gráfico digital, con algunas recomendaciones para reducir el despilfarro. La campaña está dirigida a todo tipo de restaurantes, y de momento se han unido nueve, entre ellos Semproniana, de la cocinera Ada Parellada, que ha asistido a la presentación.
Parellada ha comentado que hace tiempo que está «indignada con el despilfarro», y ha denunciado que algunos restauradores «tienen el inmenso morro» de no sólo no facilitar la reutilización de la comida sobrante sino de «criminalizarla».
En la misma línea, la Directora del Área de Prevención y Fomento del Reciclaje de la Agencia de Residuos de Cataluña, Pilar Chiva Rodríguez, ha resaltado que «despilfarrar recursos es inaceptable» y en el caso de los alimentos se añade «un componente moral o ético», porque hay «gente pasando hambre».
También ha añadido que desde el Govern se han establecido el objetivo «prioritario» de reducir el despilfarro en un 50 % en 2020. Por su parte, la Regidora de Comercio y Mercados del Ayuntamiento de Barcelona, Montserrat Ballarín, ha expresado el compromiso del gobierno municipal en hacer difusión y dar visibilidad a la campaña, de la que ha alabado el tono «positivo, no catastrofista ni moralista».

Recursos sobre horts escolars ecològics
Recopilació realitzada a partir de diversos fonts per Jordi Montagut Alandi fruit de les Pràctiques realitzades a la Diputació de Barcelona
A proposta dels membres de la Comissió d'horts socials i municipals de la Xarxa de Ciutats i Pobles cap a la Sostenibilitat, presentem una recopilació d'informació i recursos sobre horts escolars.
Index: Recursos pedagògics i experiències - Premi
Materials educatius de la xarxa d’horts escolars ecològics:
RECURSOS PER A HORTS EDUCATIUS I ESCOLARS
(de l'1 al 10 font PAEE)
- Fitxa divulgativa núm. 2: Recull de material educatiu:
- Material educatiu dedicat a l’educació ambiental dels infants per a que aquests tinguin un paper principal en conscienciar la societat i beneficiar als productors agroalimentaris. En aquest document podem trobar varies eines de treball i recursos que s’utilitzen en l’educació ambiental amb els infants.
- Alimentació. Guia informativa i proposta d’activitats per promoure l’alimentació agroecològica.
- Els horts escolars ecològics formen una iniciativa dins dels centres escolars que és veu recolzada per la cuina de l’escola i els àpats que serveixen als infants per tal de fomentar des de tot àmbit la importància de conceptes com la seguretat alimentària, el comerç just, varietats autòctones, sobirania alimentària i poder formar part d’un canvi en l’escola i convertir-se en un factor educatiu per als infants. En l’arxiu hi podeu trobar una amplia guia d’informació, eines i treball.
- A Taula! Manual per a la introducció d’aliments ecològics i de proximitat a les escoles.
- Aquesta guia té per objectiu ajudar a introduir aliments de proximitat tant a l’ambient escolar com a casa. En el següent enllaç trobareu la informació.
- Maleta Pedagògica per a l’Educació Primària i l’ESO “De l’hort a casa”.
- Material educatiu didàctic adreçat a escolars i professorat on coneixerem des dels principis de l’agricultura ecològica fins a aprendre la biodiversitat de casa nostra i adquirir la suficient autonomia com per a muntar un hort a casa.
- Exposició escolar itinerant “Que són els aliments ecològics”.
- Material educatiu que ens explica el camí dels aliments des de la seva producció fins a la seva consumició a taula, la pràctica de l’agricultura i la ramaderia, i els aliments ecològics i ecològics elaborats. Aquesta exposició itinerant (actualment en format pdf ) s’utilitza des de l’àmbit del professor a l’alumne. La podeu trobar en l’enllaç a continuació.
- Plafó 1 - Plafó 2 - Plafó 3 - Plafó 4 - Plafó 5 - Plafó 6
- Àlbum il·lustrat infantil “Que és l’agricultura ecològica?”
- Material educatiu dedicat a nens de primària des de la conscienciació i educació dels infants amb la intenció que ajudin a la protecció i conservació del medi ambient i la salut. A continuació podeu trobar aquesta eina.
- Pensem el que mengem?
- Material en forma de manual del projecte “Menjadors escolars ecològics”. Conté informació del sistema alimentari actual i els seus efectes, amb indicatius de la importància de fomentar l’agricultura i sistemes productius.
- L’Hort escolar – Guia pràctica d’horticultura ecològica -.
- Material d’eines per a docents que formin part del projecte d’un hort escolar ecològic. Guia practica de treball a l’hort. Aquest llibre, de Joan Solé i Hilda Weissmann, va ser publicat l'any 2006 pel Sector de Serveis Urbans i Medi Ambient de l'Ajuntament de Barcelona per donar eines pràctiques a tots els docents que estan desenvolupant iniciatives d'horticultura ecològica a les escoles. Així, es parla dels aspectes a tenir en compte a l'hora d'instal·lar l'hort, d'escollir les eines i estris per treballar-hi, sobre la terra, el compost, les plantes i la seva salut i sobre l'organització de la plantació. Així mateix, es proposa tot un seguit d'activitats pedagògiques per tal d'integrar l'hort a l'aula i al laboratori.
- Hort i Jardí escolar.
- Informació i àmbits per a poder tenir un hort escolar. Informació de la generalitat des de Accessoris i eines per fer un hort, un jardí sostenible, crear compostatge, una bassa com a ecosistema, millorar el pati de l’escola i l’Hort ecològic escolar i urbà.
- Curs d’hort urbà ecològic.
- Un manual d’informació de com dissenyar un hort urbà. Cura i normes a seguir. L'Àrea de Govern de Medi Ambient i Mobilitat de l'Ajuntament de Madrid, ha editat en format digital un interessant manual sobre hort urbà ecològic que aporta informació útil sobre com dissenyar un hort urbà, la seva cura i manteniment seguint les normes de l'agricultura ecològica. L'índex del contingut d'aquest manual és el següent: 1. L'hort urbà , 2. Les necessitats de les hortalisses , 3. Disseny de l'hort urbà , 4. Preparació del sòl i fertilització , 5. Sembra i Planificació , 6. Altres tasques de manteniment , 7. Descripció dels principals cultius , 8. Plagues i Malalties , 9. Tasques a l'hort al llarg de l'any , 10. Bibliografia i enllaços web d'interès.
- Agroecologia Escolar a Sant Cugat del Vallès. Recull d'Activitats d'Agroecologia Escolar (2014) / Llibre
- L'hort escolar ecològic de Vilafranca del Penedès
- Programa d'Horts escolars als centre educatius de Badalona
- Projecte d'hort de l'Escola del Mar
- Projecte d'hort CEIP Mogent
- Recurs educatiu: Les aventures de Júlia i Steven: descobrint el món de l'agricultura ecològica
Aquests enllaços ens traslladen als diferents manuals i dinàmiques que és utilitzat tant pels docents com pels alumnes per tal de donar format al per que s’insisteix en una agricultura de proximitat, km0, educació ambiental des dels més petits com a eina de transmissió a la resta, (“entre d’altres”).
En tot aquest món que ens hem endinsat, des de la xarxa d’horts escolars ecològics, és fonamenta una certa recompensa per a aquell hort escolar ecològic que aprofiti tot els recursos que se l’hi ha ofert, i un cop l’any s’ofereix el Premi Escola.
El Premi Escola, s’adreça a tots els centres d’educació infantil, primària, secundària, batxillerat, educació professional, educació especial i llar d’infants de Catalunya amb l’objectiu d’estimular tots els centris per a que emprenguin aquesta gran aposta, que no deixa de esser una eina d’educació ambiental.
Aquest guardó parteix de l’acord entre l’Associació Vida Sana i la Generalitat de Catalunya mitjançant el Departament d’Agricultura, Ramaderia, Pesca i Alimentació, i el de Ensenyament i Territori i Sostenibilitat.

title: Fundació Comtal Benet Corner - Fundació Comtal
text:
BENET CORNER
El Benet Corner és un espai comunitari obert, que convida al veïnatge i a la ciutadania en general, a desenvolupar iniciatives mediambientals, de sostenibilitat, de cura, i formació. Sempre des d’una perspectiva intercultural i/o intergeneracional i com a espai segur. L’objectiu és potenciar una millor convivència i un major sentit de pertinença al barri.
El projecte es va iniciar al 2019 quan l’Ajuntament de Barcelona ens va cedir l’espai.
El Benet Corner ocupa un perímetre de 420m2 i està situat entre el carrer Rec Comtal i el Passatge de Sant Benet. Gràcies a l’esforç col·laboratiu de les persones treballadores i ateses per la fundació i persones voluntàries del barri, el solar del Benet Corner s’ha transformat i embellit fins a convertir-se en un espai natural on poder fer vincles socials.
L’espai comunitari compta amb una zona d’hort funcional on les plantes aromàtiques i les collites de vegetals s’aprofiten en el PFI de cuina de l’Escola de Segona Oportunitats de la fundació. També disposa d’una zona infantil, una taula de ping-pong i àrees de descans.
En el Benet Corner, diferents grups de serveis socials del barri utilitzen l’espai per fer trobades i activitats comunitàries.

title: Menjador solidari Gregal – Ateneu Cooperatiu del Barcelonès Nord
text:
Menjador solidari Gregal
13 de setembre de 2023
Que ningú es quedi sense menjar
BONES PRÀCTIQUES. Destaquem bones pràctiques del cooperativisme i l’economia social i solidària que poden ser inspiradores per altres organitzacions i per a projectes que les vulguin adoptar o adaptar.
L’enfocament no assistencialista del Menjador Solidari Gregal, als barris de Besòs i Maresme de Barcelona són un exemple de com, des de l’autoorganització veïnal, resoldre les necessitats d’alimentació d’una gran quantitat de persones treballant activament per establir vincles i canviar la pròpia situació.
El Menjador Solidari Gregal va iniciar el seu recorregut l’any 2012, en un procés de reconversió de l’activitat històrica de la cooperativa Escola Gregal, SCCL, amb una clara intenció reivindicativa i de protesta popular per l’enorme deteriorament de les condicions de vida que estava experimentant el barri del Besòs i Maresme del districte Sant Martí de la ciutat de Barcelona.
La cooperativa gestiona un servei de menjador, que va començar ajudant unes poques veïnes i ara alimenta una mitjana de 400 persones cada dia. Aquest projecte forma part d’una resposta comunitària per millorar la vida de les persones, impulsant l’autoorganització i la gestió dels projectes veïnals.
L’acció de Gregal no es limita a l’assistència, sinó que busca establir relacions amb les persones de manera integral, en línia amb els principis fonamentals de l’entitat. Així, no només proporcionen una necessitat bàsica com l’alimentació, sinó que treballen activament perquè les persones puguin trobar les eines per canviar la seva situació. Aquestes accions són desenvolupades mitjançant projectes d’economia social arrelats al territori i orientats a satisfer les necessitats de les persones.
Objectius
Els objectius del Menjador solidari són els següents:
- Treballar pel bé comú en defensa de la dignitat humana, construint col·lectivament relacions justes i solidàries entre les diferents persones que conviuen en la comunitat a on intervenen.
- Promoure les capacitats personals per l’exercici de les llibertats.
- Reconèixer i defensar la riquesa de la diversitat humana com un valor imprescindible per la cohesió social, la convivència, la pau i la dignitat de les persones.
- Denunciar les injustícies i la manca de recursos individuals i col·lectius.
- Promoure la participació i la cooperació.
- Lluitar contra la discriminació i desigualtat social.
- Ser transparents en la informació, la gestió de recursos i l’impacte de les seves accions
- Adaptar-se i actuar per donar respostes innovadores i de qualitat als temps que vivim.
- Millorar la qualitat de vida i benestar de les persones del barri amb dificultats de proveir-se d’aliments tenint accés a una alimentació digne.
Context
Al 2010, amb l’agreujament de la crisi iniciada al 2008, les condicions de vida al barri del Besòs i Maresme del districte Sant Martí de la ciutat de Barcelona estaven patint un enorme deteriorament, al que la protesta popular estava donant resposta. En aquest context la històrica cooperativa Escola Gregal va iniciar un procés de reconversió de la seva activitat creant, al 2012, el Menjador Solidari Gregal.
Gregal és una cooperativa que té com a objectiu millorar la qualitat de vida al barri del Besòs i el Maresme. Des dels seus inicis com a cooperativa escolar, han estat compromesos amb la transformació social i la lluita contra la desigualtat socioeconòmica que ha afectat històricament aquesta zona. Malgrat les crisis econòmiques, han buscat superar les carències socials del barri.
La cooperativa ha aconseguit desenvolupar projectes que mostren la crua realitat del barri i, al mateix temps, demostren la solidaritat de les veïnes i altres persones compromeses
Actualment es troben en una nova seu a la Rambla Prim 76-78, amb unes instal·lacions industrials de cuina, un espai de magatzem, una sala per acollir a les persones usuàries que desitgin dinar al menjador i un despatx d’oficina.
A banda de treballar en el menjador s’han desenvolupat altres activitats alternatives, com la creació d’espais de cuina de comunitària, formació, orientació i inserció socio-laboral, el desplegament d’un dispositiu d’atenció a la salut i un punt d’assessorament socio-jurídic entre d’altres accions.
Implementació: la creació d’un menjador comunitari
L’equip del Menjador Solidari Gregal està format per 7 persones: 2 persones de logística responsables de la recollida d’aliments, 2 persones en tasques cuina, 2 treballadores socials per l’acollida de persones, dinamització de projectes, tasques administratives i comunicació. Malgrat aquesta diferenciació de tasques, funcionen de manera col·laborativa i amb horitzontalitat.
El menjador és possible gràcies a la participació de voluntariat, dels comerços i les donacions d’aliments de persones individuals. Amb aquest servei es cobreix l’àpat principal del dia a persones amb necessitats de proveir-se d’aliments. Actualment, es donen uns 400 àpats al menjador de dilluns a divendres i de carmanyoles per cobrir el cap de setmana. De les persones que accedeixen al menjador el 73,3% són homes.
Al voltant d’aquest servei s’han desenvolupat altres activitats amb els usuaris:
- Formació accessible per fomentar l’ocupació i l’exercici dels seus drets
- Espai de cuina comunitària per crear sinergia entre els usuaris del menjador, el veïnat i entitats i agents socials del territori.
- Acompanyament als usuaris en l’orientació i disseny de plans de treball enfocats a la inserció formativa i laboral.
- Tallers de cuina, per usuaris i pel veïnat. Un espai per compartir i aprendre receptes en el marc de l’aprofitament alimentari, la promoció d’hàbits alimentaris saludables i crear vincles en el territori.
- Salut sense sostre que, amb la cooperació de metges voluntaris i del CAP Besòs, s’ofereix un espai d’atenció sanitària a peu de carrer per facilitar als usuaris vinculats al Menjador Solidari Gregal l’accés a la salut a les persones que encara no disposen de targeta sanitària.
- Espai d’assessorament socio-jurídic, amb la col·laboració d’un advocat voluntari per oferir espais d’atenció i assessorament.
- Espai d’escolta a usuaris del Menjador Solidari Gregal per recollir les seves necessitats, a banda de l’alimentació i poder-los derivar a serveis o recursos del barri.
- Participació comunitària en diferents espais d’activitats del barri: mostra d’entitats, fira ESS, balanç social, sopars solidaris a la festa del barri elaborats pel taller de cuina.
- Recollida de joguines per repartir-les entre les famílies dels usuaris del Menjador Solidari Gregal.
- Participació en els centres educatius amb els projectes “menjar llibres” distribuint berenars a infants de tres centres educatius. Ja s’han realitzat tres tallers de cuina per infants.
- Xerrades sobre temes diversos: salut comunitària, presentació de llibres… propostes que han pogut trencar la barrera entre qui és usuari del menjador i qui no ho és, acabant amb prejudicis i estigmatismes que es poden tenir amb relació a les persones que assisteixen al menjador. Com a conseqüència, s’ha generat vincle i xarxa entre persones que es troben en situacions socials molt diferents, afavorint la bona convivència.
També cal destacar com a bona pràctica del Menjador Solidari Gregal el projecte ALIMENTA, ja que és un projecte innovador a escala de ciutat de Barcelona, actuant com a projecte pilot.
El projecte Alimenta ofereix :
- 30 àpats a persones residents al territori del Besòs Maresme amb dificultats
- Compta amb una persona dinamitzadora que els ofereix acompanyament i orientació als plans de treball enfocats a la formació i inserció laboral del qual ja n’han estat receptores 68 persones.
- S’han fomentat sinergies entre veïnat, agents socials i entitats del barri creant l’espai de cuina comunitària
- La compra de productes alimentaris de km0 (productors del territori, comerços del barri…)
Taller de cuina comunitària en el marc del Projecte Alimenta Taller de cuina comunitària en el marc del Projecte Alimenta Reunió de Salut Sense Sostre, Menjador Comunitari Gregal i CAP Besòs
Aprenentatges
Les activitats realitzades en el marc de la creació del menjador comunitari i altres iniciatives relacionades han proporcionat diversos aprenentatges i beneficis. A continuació es presenten alguns dels aprenentatges obtinguts:
1. Coneixement de les necessitats locals: A través del menjador comunitari, s’ha pogut obtenir una comprensió més profunda de les necessitats alimentàries de les persones del barri. Això ha permès adaptar i millorar els serveis per satisfer aquestes necessitats específiques.
2. Col·laboració i solidaritat: La participació de voluntaris i les donacions d’aliments de persones i comerços han mostrat el poder de la col·laboració i la solidaritat en la comunitat. Aquesta implicació conjunta ha estat fonamental per a l’èxit del menjador i altres activitats relacionades.
3. Oportunitats d’aprenentatge i formació: La formació accessible ofereix als usuaris l’oportunitat d’adquirir coneixements i habilitats que poden ajudar-los a millorar les seves perspectives d’ocupació i a exercir els seus drets. Això promou l’empoderament i l’autonomia dels participants.
4. Sinergies i xarxes de suport: L’espai de cuina comunitària ha creat una plataforma per a la interacció i l’intercanvi entre els usuaris del menjador, la comunitat veïnal i altres entitats socials del territori. Aquesta col·laboració ha generat sinergies positives i ha fomentat una xarxa de suport mútuament beneficiosa.
5. Accés a serveis bàsics: Els serveis d’acompanyament, com l’orientació laboral i l’assessorament socio-jurídic, han estat essencials per ajudar els usuaris a superar barreres i accedir a oportunitats laborals i de suport social. Això contribueix a millorar la seva situació i a fomentar la inclusió social.
6. Participació comunitària: La participació en els centres educatius i altres esdeveniments comunitaris ha permès establir una presència visible i integrada en el barri. Aquesta participació activa contribueix a la construcció de vincles i relacions positives amb la comunitat.
En resum, les activitats desenvolupades han proporcionat coneixement, col·laboració, oportunitats d’aprenentatge, suport comunitari i una millora en l’atenció de les necessitats dels usuaris del menjador. Això ha permès abordar més àmplies les necessitats de les persones i treballar cap a la millora de les seves condicions de vida en diferents àmbits.
Recursos, suports i aliances
Hi ha 70 persones voluntàries que col·laboren amb el Menjador Solidari Gregal.
El pressupost global pel menjador solidari Gregal pel 2022 procedeix del 85% de la subvenció Ajuntament de Barcelona. El 15% restant del total, va a càrrec de la cooperativa amb la seva activitat econòmica.
A banda d’aquests fons de finançament, durant l’any 2022 es va iniciar la línia de serveis de càtering el territori de Sant Martí la qual ha generat uns beneficis que es preveu que incrementin amb el transcurs del temps.
El menjador també és possible per la col·laboració de les següents entitats i programes: STM Mantenimiento, EO.L. Service, Mikonta, Coop57, casal Ca l’Isidret, Faura-Casas, Zurich, Banc dels Aliments i Pla de Barris. El Menjador està enxarxat també amb altres entitats, equipaments i organitzacions que conjuntament promouen l’acció i la participació comunitària al barri de Besòs i el Maresme: l’Hotel W, la Fundació PareManel, Cultivar SA, Rotary Club i l’Hoac del Besòs i la Pau, bombers del Poblenou.

title: Jardí Fènix - ABD
description: El Jardí Fènix, es una iniciativa de agricultura urbana para mejorar la ocupabilidad de las personas en tratamiento de drogodependencias
text:
Inicio » Programes » Jardí Fènix
Jardí Fènix
El Jardí Fènix, es una iniciativa de agricultura urbana para mejorar la ocupabilidad de las personas en tratamiento de drogodependencias. En un contexto donde el estigma y la exclusión social son realidades comunes, esta iniciativa se propone no solo mejorar la ocupabilidad de este colectivo, sino también empoderarlos a través de la agricultura urbana. Al combinar formación, trabajo práctico y la creación de una comunidad de apoyo, el proyecto busca transformar la vida de sus participantes, dándoles las herramientas necesarias para reintegrarse con éxito en la sociedad.
A medida que la población se enfrenta a crisis sociales y de salud mental, es fundamental desarrollar enfoques innovadores que fomenten la inclusión y el bienestar. La agroecología, como modelo de producción sostenible, se presenta como una alternativa valiosa para generar conciencia medioambiental y fomentar habilidades que son esenciales en el mundo laboral actual. Al involucrar a las personas en el proceso de cultivo y cuidado de plantas, se fomenta no solo el desarrollo de habilidades técnicas, sino también la creación de vínculos afectivos y de confianza en sí mismos.
Este enfoque también permite una reflexión profunda sobre la relación que tenemos con la alimentación y el medio ambiente. A través de la práctica de la agroecología, los participantes aprenderán sobre la importancia del consumo responsable y la sostenibilidad, convirtiéndose en agentes de cambio en sus propias comunidades. Bajo el lema Cultivando nuevas oportunidades, El Jardí Fènix se erige como una plataforma para la transformación personal y colectiva, creando un espacio donde se valora la dignidad y el potencial de cada individuo.
Objetivos:
A través de una formación integral en agroecología, el Jardí Fènix busca proporcionar a los participantes las habilidades y competencias necesarias para acceder a oportunidades laborales en el sector agrícola y en áreas relacionadas con la sostenibilidad. Esto incluye el aprendizaje práctico sobre cultivo, manejo de productos agrícolas y técnicas de jardinería, así como el desarrollo de habilidades de trabajo en equipo y gestión del tiempo.
El Jardí Fènix tiene como objetivo desafiar y desmantelar los prejuicios asociados con las personas en tratamiento de drogodependencias. A través de la visibilización de sus logros y el trabajo colaborativo con la comunidad, se busca crear un entorno de aceptación y respeto, fomentando la comprensión de que cada individuo tiene un potencial valioso que puede contribuir al bienestar social.
El Jardí Fènix aspira a ser un espacio abierto y accesible para la comunidad del barrio de Sarrià-Sant Gervasi. A través de actividades colaborativas y eventos comunitarios, se buscará fomentar la interacción entre los participantes del proyecto y los vecinos, promoviendo un sentido de pertenencia y cohesión social. Esto incluye la organización de talleres, charlas y actividades al aire libre que fomenten el conocimiento sobre agroecología y sostenibilidad.
A través de la educación y la práctica en agroecología, el Jardí Fènix busca sensibilizar a los participantes y a la comunidad en general sobre la importancia de un consumo responsable. Al cultivar sus propios alimentos, los participantes aprenderán sobre la procedencia de los productos y la necesidad de adoptar prácticas sostenibles, contribuyendo así a la construcción de un sistema alimentario más justo y equitativo. La producción agroecológica del Jardí Fènix es donada de forma solidaria al proyecto de justicia alimentaria “La Botiga”.
Reconociendo que el proceso de recuperación es complejo, el Jardí Fènix también tiene como objetivo ofrecer un entorno seguro y de apoyo donde los participantes puedan compartir sus experiencias, desafíos y logros. La creación de una red de apoyo entre los participantes fomentará la empatía y la solidaridad, lo que facilitará su reintegración social y laboral.
Desarrollo del Proyecto
Bajo el lema Cultivando nuevas oportunidades, el Jardí Fènix acompaña a unas 50 personas durante el año. Las personas participantes se involucran en todo el proceso: desde el cultivo y mantenimiento de las plantas, utilizando un modelo de jardinería forestal, hasta la organización del trabajo, la planificación productiva. Para ello, se ofrecen formaciones básicas en agroecología, así como un acompañamiento ocupacional en función de un itinerario de inserción social personalizado.
Este enfoque no solo capacita a los participantes en habilidades ocupacionales prácticas, sino que también les ofrece bienestar emocional, mejorando sus posibilidades de superar la adicción. Además, les brinda experiencia en emprendimientos socio-productivos, fomentando su autosuficiencia al producir sus propios alimentos y su solidaridad con proyectos de justicia alimentaria. Al mismo tiempo, se promueve el consumo responsable y el desarrollo de un sistema alimentario sostenible.
Impacto Comunitario
Además de los beneficios individuales para las personas en tratamiento de drogodependencias, el Jardí Fènix tiene una importante vertiente comunitaria. El jardín se propone como un espacio de intercambio y colaboración para entidades y vecinos del distrito. Se fomenta la realización de actividades al aire libre, encuentros familiares y visitas de escuelas o proyectos de ocio interesados en la agroecología social. Asimismo, se instala un punto de información sobre ecología alimentaria accesible para toda la comunidad, con el objetivo de romper prejuicios y estigmas relacionados con las adicciones.
La colaboración con el Colegio de Arquitectos de Cataluña (COAC) fue clave, ya que se encargó del arreglo y mejora de algunos de los espacios del proyecto.
Proyecto
El proyecto Fénix es una iniciativa de agroecología urbana cuyo objetivo principal es mejorar la inclusión social y laboral de personas en tratamiento de drogodependencias, al mismo tiempo que trabaja para romper el estigma asociado a estas situaciones. Este proyecto se lleva a cabo en el jardín del Centro de Atención y Seguimiento (CAS) de Sarrià, un espacio cedido por parte del Ayuntamiento de Barcelona
El proyecto recibe financiación por parte del Departamento de Derechos sociales e inclusión de la Generalitat de Catalunya y del Departamento de Salud, como también apoyo del Ayuntamiento de Barcelona.

title: Xaingra. Xarxa d'Intercanvi – Ateneu Rosa de Foc
text:
La Xarxa d’Intercanvi de Gràcia és una unió voluntària i lliure de veïns i veïnes del barri de Gràcia que han decidit complementar les seves activitats econòmiques “habituals” (béns, serveis i coneixements) amb intercanvis solidaris informals, sense usar diner. Aquesta xarxa neix a partir de la inconformitat amb el sistema econòmic en el que vivim, amb un esperit de transformació social.
Des de Xaingra sempre s’ha entès que l’economia ha d’estar al servei de les persones i no a l’inrevés. Els objectius de la xarxa són:
- Potenciar relaciones més humanes entre veïns i veïnes.
- Portar a la pràctica un exemple de resistència i alternativa al consumisme desmesurat i no sostenible, i al malbaratament en la nostra societat amb profundes desigualtats socials.
- Crear major teixit associatiu crític a nivell local.
- Potenciar que tots i totes tenim molt que aprendre i molt que aportar o ensenyar.
- Educar-nos en els valors de reciprocitat, tolerància, flexibilitat, gratuïtat i esperit de col·lectivitat.
Xaingra funciona de forma física en mercats d’intercanvi, i de forma virtual a través de llistes de correu electrònic i grup de Whatsapp.
Mercats: Varies vegades a l’any organitzem a la plaça de la Virreina del barri de Gràcia un mercat d’intercanvi on desenes de persones passen un dia sense diners intercanviant bens i serveis. Paral.lelament solen realitzar-se activitats de sensibilització i lluita, lúdiques i creatives, proposades per entitats o persones a títol individual. Generalment la Xarxa d’Aliments ofereix aperitiu i dinar a partir del reciclatge d’aliments.
Comencem el mercat muntant les taules entre totes.Es tracte que la gent porti qualsevol objecte, nou o vell que ja no faci servir (roba, mobles, joguines, llibres, discos, electrodomèstics, menjar…) i ho canviï per una altra cosa que necessiti o l’agradi. També es poden intercanviar serveis i coneixements.
LLista de correu: Tenim dues llistes de correu, una per a fer ofertes i demandes d’intercanvis i rebre informació, i una altra només per a informar de les nostres activitats.
Pots apuntar-te a la llista d’ofertes i demandes d’intercanvis a:
https://llistes.moviments.net/listinfo/xaingra
I a la de noticies i informacions vàries:
https://llistes.moviments.net/listinfo/info-xaingra
Grup de whatsapp: escriu a xaingra@rosadefoc.info i t’informarem de com accedir. Tenim un límit de 250 persones.
La xarxa és una iniciativa sorgida de l’Ateneu Rosa de foc (espai d’acció i pensament crític de la Vila de Gràcia – http://ateneurosadefoc.wordpress.com/ )
Pots veure algunes fotos de mercats a les galeries d’imatges d’aquesta web.

description: Our video introduction to this year's Christmas Cheer
text:
|
Our video introduction to this year's Christmas Cheer |
|
One ActivityOver the years we have been able to build relationships with many families, who have been empowered to succeed. With the help of numerous partners, we have been able to bless many families in Brighton and Hove and beyond through our Christmas Cheer Project. We have provided hampers to families who most need the help and support over the Christmas period.
The individuals, organisations and churches appreciate that their donations go to people we are in relationship with and they value this principle. From the feedback received it is evident that families very much appreciate and value the Christmas hampers, especially with the rising cost of energy. Many recipients shared the contents of the hamper with other friends and family. |
Many RecipientsFor Christmas 2025, the ongoing global, ever-increasing cost of living has had an effect on all of us. So, we knew that when requesting donations of any kind, we would be a facing challenge. Donations were slow and at times the demand appeared impossible to meet. However, we were able to put together the donations received, which then overall directly benefited a whopping 529 individuals!
It is good to note that each year the referrals receive 1to1 assessment which will check eligibility and enable us to understand the needs of that household. No one is automatically put on our list. The hampers are tailor made for each recipient/ household. These came in 5 categories of hamper types: 1)gifts and toys, 2) Christmas luxury foods 3) Toiletries 4) long life, non-perishable foods, 5) Christmas dinner. Christmas Cheer 2025 provided the following. - 74 households received gifts and toy hampers given, benefitting 220 individuals.
- 26 households received Christmas luxury foods benefitting 73 individuals
- 26 households received toiletries with 70 individuals benefitting
- 27 households received long life, non-perishables. Benefitting 70 individuals
- 22 Christmas dinner hampers where 96 individuals enjoyed the festive meal.
We want to particularly thank A SHARE OF THE CROP who, for the third year running, provided vegetables and fruit for the food hampers, and to the company MPB who gave us three teams of volunteers over 3 days, who really acted as a catalyst in the mammoth hamper task we faced! We received donations of new gifts and monies from individuals, organisations and churches in the Sussex area including Thumbprint Foundation. Appreciation was expressed not only for the hampers but also for the human interaction as the hampers were delivered or collected. (See below for the feedback received). |

title: Welcome - Fitzherbert Community Hub
description: Our mission: to reduce food poverty and social isolation by welcoming and nourishing all with food, friendship and fun. A safe place to eat, form lasting relationships, exercise and belong.
text:
Welcome to the Fitzherbert Community Hub! A community of communities, a sanctuary where the diverse people of East Brighton can connect and thrive.
Our mission is to reduce food poverty and social isolation, progressively and determinedly, by welcoming and nourishing all with food, friendship and fun; offering a safe place where local people can come to eat, form lasting relationships, exercise and belong.
We have converted the parish hall and courtyard at St John the Baptist church into a Community Hub and City Garden with a commercial standard teaching kitchen, dining area, purpose-built food bank facilities and additional meeting spaces designed to promote activity and instil a sense of belonging in your local area.
A place where you can get together with your neighbours and get to know them better. Real Junk Food Project Brighton are running a ‘pay as you feel’ community café from the Hub using food that would otherwise be sent to landfill. The café is open Tuesday to Friday: 10.00 – 14.00 (Lunch is served from 12.00).
You can make a donation to the project by contacting us here.
We’re now celebrating our 3rd anniversary! Find out more…
What’s on at the Hub
The Fitz Cafe
The Community Cafe is run by The Real Junk Food Project Brighton and serves barista coffee, cakes and pastries from 10am. Join us from noon for a delicious lunch made from food that would otherwise go to waste on a ‘pay as you feel basis’
Opening times:
Tuesday to Friday: 10.00-14.00 (lunch from noon)
mASCot Mondays Cafe at the Fitzherbert Hub
mASCot Mondays @Fitz is an invitation only lunch club, run by volunteers, many of whom are neuro divergent. As always you will find a welcoming team offering nourishing food on a pay as you feel basis.
Monday: mASCot training session (places are limited – contact us for an invitation)
Citizens Advice Sessions
We have Advice Sessions by Citizens Advice the first Wednesday of each month during cafe hours.
Enquire in the cafe.
Foodbank at the Fitzherbert Hub
The Food bank is open on Mondays in the Presbytery – access is from the front door.
Foodbank opening times:
Monday: 10.30-11.30
Community Garden on Upper Bedford Street
We have our own gardening plot on the green opposite BTTC. TRJFP welcomes volunteers who wish to help grow vegetables and herbs for the kitchen.
Enquire in the cafe.
IT/Computer training
IT/Computer training drop-in sessions at the Fitzherbert Hub. Appointments can also be arranged at the front-of-house desk.
IT/Computer Training drop-in sessions:
Drop in on Thursdays: 10:30-12:30
After School Club
Our After School Club is a winning combination of Table Tennis at BTTC and cookery lessons from The Real Junk Food Project.
After School Club runs during school terms on Mondays and Thursdays and is currently full – please contact us to join the waiting list.
Brighton Table Tennis Club at the Fitzherbert Community Hub
The cafe has become a perfect base for welcoming new players and visitors to the Brighton Table Tennis Club and sharing social time with them before and after our sessions.
Event Hire
If you would like to hire the Hub for an event, please get in touch.
Food Bank Donations
Our thanks go to the Brighton & Hove Food Partnership, FareShare Sussex, Sussex Gleaning Network, The Real Junk Food Project Brighton, Brighton Food Factory, Brighton & Hove City Council, the SVP Our Lady of Lourdes, Rottingdean and the Albert Gubay Foundation for food donations.
If you have any questions about food at the Fitzherbert Community Hub or you’d like to make a donation, you can get in touch via our contact page. Click the button below
You can also find more information about the Emergency Food Network in Brighton & Hove here.
Latest News & stories
We are two!
January saw the celebration of the second anniversary of the Fitzherbert Community Hub. As we start a new year it is perfect time to reflect on our achievements and aspirations for the year ahead and beyond.
Last year we talked of success being a result of the commitment and aspiration of all partners towards community integration and social value. We are delighted that we have seen that manifested in action throughout another year with passion and conviction. Activities in the Fitz have reflected the diversity and enterprise of our community.
We have been experimental and inventive but within our safe space. We have been busy, purposeful and also had fun.
Find out more about our achievements and plans for the future here.
After School Club at BTTC and the Hub – Watch Video by Stories of Note
Check out the latest video from local filmmaker Stories of Note – this one shows the after school club at the hub and Brighton Table Tennis Club. You can see more short films documenting the development of the Fitzherbert Community Hub, here.
The Fitzherbert Blog
For updates on the Fitzherbert Community Hub project, fundraising news, information about what’s on at the Hub and the latest from our partners, check out the blog here.
We did it! £18K raised on Crowdfunder
On 2 February 2024 we successfully raised £18,104 with 100 supporters in 60 days.
A huge thank you to all who donated to our Crowdfunder.
Support The Fitzherbert Community Hub Winter Crowdfunder
With only days left to go, we have almost reached our Winter Crowdfunder target. You can help us reach that target by making a pledge and helping us spread the word.
Veganuary Fundraiser
Celebrate Veganuary with The Real Junk Food Project at the Fitzherbert Community Hub at our first Supper Club on Saturday 27 January. Tickets on sale now.
Find out about our partners
Brighton Table Tennis Club, Real Food Project Brighton, Voices in Exile and St John the Baptist Church are working together on the Fitzherbert Community Hub project with a shared vision to reduce food poverty and social isolation in East Brighton.

title: The MEP Community Garden – The Migrant English Project
text:
MEP has been teaching gardening and horticultural skills since 2010, primarily at the Roedale Valley Allotments site in Brighton. During lessons, MEP volunteer teachers introduce horticultural language within the context of tending a garden, and growing and cooking vegetables, and the allotment provides a space to put this knowledge into action.
Sessions at the allotment help students to learn new vocabulary, participate in physical activity and develop new skills. Being in a natural environment and engaging with healthy lifestyles are also beneficial for mental health, confidence and self-esteem. Crops grown are decided in a participatory manner, based on the plants students like to grow, foods they like to eat and experiences of gardening in other countries. There is an emphasis on producing fruits and vegetables for students to eat nutritional meals – both in their own homes and in shared MEP lunches.
In 2024, the plot was officially converted from shared access to our exclusive use as the MEP Community Garden. During the Spring and Summer months, we host many joyful gardening sessions – providing tea, snacks and transport costs for MEP students and their families. We are now developing a sensory garden at the Community Garden and plant beds for students to develop their own growing spaces.
The MEP Community Garden is managed by volunteers, and we are always looking for new people to get involved, especially as plans and site usage expands. If you are interested in helping, please contact the Migrant English Project by email at mepbrighton12@gmail.com with “FAO MEP Community Garden” in the subject line.

title: YMCA Youth Advice Centre's sustainable food market: Everything you need to know - YMCA DownsLink Group
description: The Food Market has been set up in partnership with Brighton & Hove City Council, Brighton & Hove Food Partnership, FareShare Sussex, Neighbourly,
text:
In 2022, YMCA YAC Brighton have opened a Youth-Led sustainable social grocery store for anyone aged 16-25, living in the Brighton and Hove area.
The Food Market has been set up in partnership with Brighton & Hove City Council, Brighton & Hove Food Partnership, FareShare Sussex, Neighbourly, Brighton & Hove Food Factory, and Sussex University.
The aim of the Food Market is to support young people in accessing healthy, low-cost foods and shopping products at a simple one-stop shop. It is an easy way for young people who struggle to afford the rising cost of goods to access as well as providing a modern and sustainable approach to food waste and food poverty.
The Food Market is not a foodbank. However, we are able to provide free groceries to those who are in need in a positive and empowering way. This is supported by the sales from paying customers and/or solidarity fees. These meals will support our community of young people who may be rough sleeping, in emergency accommodation, young families, or those with other emergency food needs.
How does the Food Market work?
Young people pay a small fee, and in return they will be able to access a week’s worth of fresh produce and stock cupboard items.
Young people can visit the Food Market on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays between 3pm-5pm at 11 St Georges Place, BN1 4GB.
How much does it cost?
- 12 items for £5
- You can come once a week
- An option to pay more in support of young people experiencing food poverty
- Occasional free items available
Where does the food come from?
Most of the food at YAC Food Market comes from local supermarkets. Some of the food will be provided through donations from local businesses.
FAQ’s
How much does it cost?
- £5.00 per shop
Who can use it?
- Anyone within the age range of 16-25
- When is it open?
- Tuesday – Thursday 2PM – 5PM
What if I have allergies?
- If it is your fist time using the food market you’ll be asked to fill in a form. On the form will be a section all to do with food allergies/intolerance/preferences. We try to have a wide range of products to cater for all.

title: Home - Capuchin Day Centre
text:
Capuchin Day Centre
for homeless people
No-One Goes Hungry
The Capuchin Day Centre has been providing homeless supports in Dublin for over 57 years.
Founded in 1969 by Capuchin friar, Brother Kevin Crowley, and inspired by the spirit of St Francis Assisi, the Centre was set up to ‘relieve the hardship endured by homeless people.
Situated in Bow Street, Dublin 7, the Day Centre started out providing meals for the homeless in Dublin and has developed its services over the years to meet the presenting needs of those who come seeking food and support.
From hot meals, food parcels, showering facilities and clothing to medical, optical, dental and family services, the Capuchin Day Centre is committed to providing practical, meaningful support to those who seek help.
Those who come to the Day Centre for support are considered to be our guests. They are welcomed without judgement and are served on a “no questions asked” basis.
In line with the values of the Irish Capuchin Friars the Centre works on the principle that no one should go hungry and offers support that is non-judgemental, open to all, and places the dignity and respect of our guests at the heart of what we do.
OUR HELP IN NUMBERS
In 2025 we provided
Food and Meal Services
We serve approximately 350 guests for breakfast and 700 people for dinner each day and distribute over 1400 food parcels each week.
Medical and Hygiene Services
Our onsite team of clinical professionals supports the health and well-being of homeless people. We also provide washing and showering facilities, haircuts and clean clothes.
Family Support Services
From infant packs with baby formula and nappies, to children’s toys, school bags and books, we help ease the broader needs of families in food poverty. These essential interventions are complemented by health-related supports from our onsite clinical team and initiatives that promote social inclusion by our family support service.

title: Cherry Orchard Community Garden by Fran Brady – Eco-Congregation Ireland
text:
Fran Brady, Quaker representative on the ECI committee, wrote this article:
Cherry Orchard Community Garden was set up in 2010 by the Cherry Orchard Regeneration Board with funding from Dublin City Council and assistance from City Dublin Vocational Educational Committee (now the Education and Training Board).
Management of the garden was handed over to the Ballyfermot/Chapelizod Partnership in 2012. It is still supported by the partnership as well as a group of enthusiastic and trained volunteers. Dublin City Council and the Department of Rural and Community Affairs later funded a Garden Manager to develop this social enterprise, centred on supplying fresh vegetables, herbs and flowers.
Cherry Orchard Community Gardensare passionate about sustainable, healthy, locally grown food that is good for the neighbourhood and good for the planet. Their aim is to be sustainable with low energy inputs, low food miles and a low carbon footprint. Fresh seasonal produce is grown using traditional gardening techniques and no artificial chemicals. As part of their sustainability journey, they will be applying for Organic producer status with the Irish Organic Association.
The Community Garden provides an amenity for local residents and volunteers, including training and employment opportunities. SVP and groups such as the Ballyfermot-Chapelizod Partnership have been responding to ‘culinary illiteracy’ with the Partnership regularly hosting classes such as ‘Healthy Food Made Easy’. To further address cooking illiteracy, SVP and Cherry Orchard Community Garden are combining their resources to provide allotment land to a number of service users. The community garden is willing to show people how to plant and grow and also organise regular gardening classes.

title: Mother McAuley Centre | Our Lady of Good Counsel
description: The Mother Catherine McAuley Centre, on Curlew Road, Drimnagh, is the Parish Centre of Our Lady of Good Counsel Parish. It opened in 1975 and provides pleasant surroundings where older persons can m
text:
The Mother Catherine McAuley Centre, on Curlew Road, Drimnagh, is the Parish Centre of Our Lady of Good Counsel Parish. It opened in 1975 and provides pleasant surroundings where older persons can meet together, enjoy a chat, play Bingo, be entertained and have a daily meal. Some of its members first came to Drimnagh to settle down and raise a family in the 1930’s. The Centre is named after the Foundress of the Sisters of Mercy (RSM).
The Sisters came to Mourne Road in 1944. Over the years they made an enormous contribution to the Drimnagh community, in the Schools and Parish. The Mother McAuley Centre was founded by the Sisters in collaboration with the Parish and the many volunteers who over the years have always ensured a professional and caring service is available to the elderly of our community. For many years the Centre has operated with assistance from the statutory services and major fundraising efforts by the volunteers. A Management Committee oversees the operation of the McAuley Centre. As well as welcoming our seniors to the Centre everyday, our local Meals on Wheels service operates from the Mc Auley.
Regretfully, the Sisters closed the convent in 2006, but the ministry to the elderly continues in the McAuley Centre. In December 2006 the Girls National School organised a special event to celebrate the work of the Sisters in the parish. An oak tree was planted on the school grounds facing the Convent of Mercy site to honour the Sisters. Many sisters who taught in Mourne Road as well as retired teachers and past pupils attended the ceremony in the school hall.
Venerable Catherine McAuley
Catherine Elizabeth McAuley was born in North Dublin in 1778. Following the death of her father in 1783, life for her became difficult both economically and socially. As a teenager she nursed her mother through a prolonged illness until she died. After that, economic circumstances necessitated moving from one relative to another in order to have a roof over her head. Sometimes this meant being separated from her brother and sister.
In 1803, Mr. and Mrs.William Callaghan, a wealthy childless couple adopted her. She moved with them to live in Coolock in the outskirts of Dublin. While she was living with them she commenced her mission of mercy to the neighbouring poor and sick. In addition she nursed Mrs. Callaghan through a lengthy illness until she died in 1819 and subsequently nursed Mr. Callaghan before his death in 1822. The Callaghan estate was left to Catherine McAuley and she used it to fund her building development in Baggot Street for the care of the poor and socially disadvantaged.
In 1831 she founded the Sisters of Mercy, a Religious Congregation largely involved in the care of the poor, the sick and educationally disadvantaged. In the early days her work was mostly among the people of Dublin, but in time the Congregation spread and became one of the largest Congregations of women, not alone in Ireland, but in the world.
Catherine McAuley was a woman of great vision. She was an innovator in what she did, but also in how she did things. The care of the sick was always close to her heart and so in 1832, when an outbreak of cholera in Dublin was claiming hundreds of lives and people fled in fear of succumbing to the disease, she organised a team of Sisters to care for the sick at an improvised hospital in Townsend Street.
Her life as a Sister of Mercy only spanned ten years. In that time she worked tirelessly to respond to the need of the poor and sick. She set up a number of foundations for this purpose both in Ireland and England and was about to make her first foundation in America when illness overtook her. She died in 1841.
She was a woman of prayer and of deep faith. Her philosophy was “Let us take one day only in the hands at a time, merely making a resolve for tomorrow. Thus we may hope to go on, taking short, careful steps, not great strides … Each day is a step we take towards Eternity … The final step will bring us into the presence of God”
Prayer of Catherine McAuley
My God
I am yours
For time and eternity
Teach me to cast myself entirely
Into the arms of
Your loving providence
With the most lively, unlimited
Confidence in your
Compassionate, tender pity.
Grant me,
O most merciful redeemer
That whatever you ordain or permit
May be acceptable to me.
Take from my heart
All painful anxiety;
Suffer nothing to sadden me but sin,
Nothing to delight me
But the hope of coming
To the possession of you
My God and my all,
In your everlasting kingdom.
Amen.

Conservation Through Use
As guardians of Ireland’s rich food heritage, we protect and preserve rare, traditional seed varieties, heritage apples, and the invaluable cultural knowledge they carry. By embracing sustainable practices and sharing these treasures, we not only safeguard the past but also nurture a thriving future for generations to come.
Heritage Seed Catalogue
Discover a carefully curated selection of organic and heritage seed varieties in our 2026 catalogue. Whether you’re a seasoned gardener or just starting your journey, you’ll find the seeds to grow a thriving, diverse garden that honours both tradition and sustainability.
Join Irish Seed Savers

What We Do at
Irish Seed Savers
From our conservation sites in County Clare, we support a growing movement of people who believe in biodiversity, community, and food sovereignty. We save seeds. We grow trees. We teach. We connect people to Ireland’s food legacy. Through our national Seed Bank, heritage orchards, education programmes, and Seed Guardian network, we keep genetic diversity alive — in gardens, fields, and farms across the country.
Conservation
Maintaining a living heritage seed bank and orchard, preserving open-pollinated seeds and fruit varieties for future generations.
Protection
Safeguarding heritage crops from environmental threats through stewardship, policy support, and strong advocacy efforts.
Utilisation
Ensuring heritage crops thrive through broad use, traditional knowledge, appropriate technology, and resilient food systems.
Education
Inspiring all ages to reconnect with nature, learn sustainable growing, conserve biodiversity, and strengthen local food systems.
Heritage, open-pollinated vegetable varieties carefully preserved and protected in our Living Seed Bank.
Ireland’s only national heritage collection of Irish apple tree varieties conserved in our orchards.
Dedicated to conserving traditional Irish crop diversity and heritage seeds since 1991.

Native Irish seeds are grown and saved annually to safeguard biodiversity and future food security.
Rooted in Heritage,

ISSA began with a simple but vital purpose: to protect Ireland’s rapidly diminishing food crop heritage from extinction. title: London’s green fingers: How Extinction Rebellion is turning protest into guerrilla gardening | One Earth
description: Discover how London activists are transforming vacant spaces into thriving urban gardens through guerrilla gardening and climate action.
text:
London’s green fingers: How Extinction Rebellion is turning protest into guerrilla gardening
The sun is setting over the concrete and bricks lining Hackney's streets in east London. On the side of a pavement sits a cardboard box, with the words “free salad” written on the front.
The lettuce was grown just behind the wire fence in a community garden - an oasis among London's grey estates. Inside, makeshift planters hold vibrant flowers, and edible salad leaves in beds. A greenhouse made out of mismatched planks of wood and glass panes can barely contain the overgrown tomato plants.
The Garden of Earthly Delights is one of London’s newest community gardens. The capital has seen a rise in edible gardens in recent years; now more than 2,500 are officially registered, as communities band together to grow their own veg in the face of food insecurity, push for more green spaces, and tackle climate change one courgette at a time.
This temporary garden in Hackney is the work of Extinction Rebellion, the activist group that's blocked streets and held rallies in an attempt to hold governments accountable over their inaction on climate change.
One month ago the Hackney group decided to extend their approach to environmental activism to the community. They found a small patch of derelict land awaiting development in a heavily urbanized and populated area, and moved in with shovels, soil and all things green.
Volunteers built plant beds with discarded planks and leftover wooden pallets, all the tools and equipment sourced from fellow XR members and friends. Vegetables grown here will be offered for the community for free. Picnic benches have been placed among the plants to invite locals to use this space as their own.
“It’s as much as about showing people how to grow their own food, how much they can make out of a small space, but also teaching about global warming and the climate crisis."
Small, urban farms, edible gardens and allotments all have their place in tackling global warming, and defending people and cities from the effects of a changing climate.
A 2016 study from the Johns Hopkins Center for a Livable Future found that urban agriculture could "increase social capital, community well-being and civic engagement with the food system," while enhancing food security, ecosystems, and improving the health and wellbeing of residents.
Writing on the subject for EcoWatch, scientist and environmental activist Dr David Suzuki said: “Local and urban agriculture can help reduce greenhouse gas emissions and recycle nutrient-rich food scraps, plant debris and other ‘wastes’.”
“Cities will be at the forefront when it comes to climate change,” says Sally Morgan, co-author of The Climate Change Garden.
While London’s guerilla gardeners are aware these green patches won’t solve the city’s environmental problems, small changes are possible and can have a ripple effect throughout communities.
These spaces have a huge potential to influence how people think about food and sustainability – and at the very least the value of green space and nature.
“It’s about giving green space for the community to use,” says Auberon Bayley, operations manager of Cultivate London, a social enterprise and urban farm. He manages various sites across west London, where young, unemployed people are taught landscaping, horticulture and how to grow food.
We meet at a pocket of green in the centre of an apocalyptic-like building site in Acton, a neighborhood that’s undergoing rapid redevelopment.
Council homes have been ripped apart and families moved in place of new buildings and housing. But this small garden has managed to stay surrounded by all of this change.
“Here we grow edibles, vegetables and wildlife spaces. The more people come along and do a little bit of planting, the more they’ll start to take that back with what they’re doing. Their balconies could be used, any little space,” says Bayley.
Although he acknowledges urban agriculture won’t solve climate change and our inefficient food system, Bayley has witnessed young people from the area who previously had no interest in horticulture develop a serious passion for gardens, green spaces and growing their own food. This, he says, is very powerful.

title: Sowing Roots: Esiah Levy - Garden Museum
text:
“Nobody knew he was going to pass away” she explained, “he went to hospital when his lower back was hurting him, and he collapsed. His wife called the ambulance.”
Esiah and Syreeta’s father came to the UK from Jamaica as a teenager. Their mum was born in the UK and her parents had come from Jamaica. Syreeta describes her father as a disciplinarian. He liked to garden and grew vegetables, leaving little space for his children to play without fear of damaging his plants. She remembers “sweetcorn, there was always tomatoes growing, there was mint … strawberries, onions, runner beans.” Syreeta thinks that food growing is a skill that “people brought with them from India, Jamaica or whatever, just the whole cultivation, rather than just having a Tesco down the road.”
Syreeta thinks that her brother started gardening when he bought his house in Croydon. He ‘was at his calmest when he was in this garden.” He also had an allotment. When Syreeta went travelling to Thailand, Malaysia, Cambodia, Vietnam, Esiah would ask her to bring seeds back, like unusual tomato varieties, “I’d get him a little seed as a souvenir, he liked to have seeds”.
Her fondest memory of her brother growing up was watching him go through different phases “but one thing he stuck to, I have to give him credit, was the gardening.” She thinks that gardening was even more important to him after he became a dad, “I think his son being born was the catalyst that helped him to look at food and growing food…. I think that was more his passion, his little boy incentivised him to grow stuff and eat healthy”. She believes that he was trying to show his son that “you can actually grow your own food and be resourceful, and things can be recycled”.

text:
The London Freedom Seed Bank is a London-wide network of seed savers, community gardeners and
food justice activists dedicated to saving, storing and distributing open-pollinated seed varieties.
It was created in 2012, by Azul Thomé and others, in response to Vandana Shiva’s worldwide call to occupy and protect seed heritage.
Today, it is volunteer-run by a team of 4 people: Charlotte Dove (co-director), Julie Riehl (co-director), Helene Schulze (co-director) and Richard Galpin (Steering Group member).
The London Freedom Seed Bank began by hosting 7 workshops over 12 months with over 50 Freedom Seed Savers. These workshops taught the value of attention to seed and the skills of seed saving.
At the end of each workshop, participants selected a packet of seed with the promise to return some seeds the following year. This first return of saved seed was marked with a festival in October 2013, gathering around 150 people.
Since then, the London Freedom Seed Bank works on several fronts.
First, raising awareness of the politics of the global seed regime and the importance of seed sovereignty, through talks, workshops, film screenings and seed storytelling circles.
Second, it aims to reskill urban food growers and gardeners with the ability to grow, save and store organic seed, creating a growing network of Freedom Seed Savers. With these savers, they maintain a living collection, of around 30-40 varieties of London-grown seeds. These seeds are shared and distributed for free to all who want to grow food.
Through its activities, the London Freedom Seed Bank deeply promotes collaboration and partnership.
It organizes workshops and publishes short pieces on its website, that you can download for free – “Introduction to seed saving”; “Saving Lettuce Seed”; “Small-scale Seed Processing and Storage”, etc.
It travels to community events throughout the year to share skills and seeds and offer their home-made seed cleaner to anyone who needs it.
In 2018, the London Freedom Seed Bank also participated in the Global Generation’s Seeds for a Better World project, the aim of which was to facilitate knowledge sharing between young and older seed savers.
The London Freedom Seed Bank collaborated by building a mobile seed bank, holding 20 different London-saved varieties. It was conceived as a discovery tool, interactive and tactile, allowing people to “pour the seeds into their hands for closer inspection whilst listening to the stories of those who have saved them”.

title: Press release: Charity urges all parties to commit to national fruit and veg on prescription programmes - Alexandra Rose
description: The first UK trial of GPs prescribing fruit and vegetables has shown promising results, leading to the charity behind the project to call for nationwide programmes to boost health and reduce food poverty. Read...
text:
The first UK trial of GPs prescribing fruit and vegetables has shown promising results, leading to the charity behind the project to call for nationwide programmes to boost health and reduce food poverty.
Alexandra Rose Charity, is currently running fruit and veg on prescriptions pilots in two London Boroughs, released findings this week sharing the profound impact the project has had on the lives of people on low incomes, living with long-term health conditions linked to poor diet.
After just 8 months of receiving vouchers for fruit and veg, 80% of participants are eating five portions of fruit and veg each day, compared to just 28% at the start of the programme. The health impacts of this change are striking: 9 in 10 participants have seen their physical health improve, including healthy weight loss, higher energy levels and better digestion. Additionally, 7 in 10 people with high blood pressure saw an improvement as recorded by doctors and nurses. Over half of participants shared that their mental health has also improved as they worry less about money for food. With support from social prescribers and healthcare professionals, these positive changes have collectively resulted in a 40% reduction in GP visits.
“Food related ill health costs the UK £98 Billion[1] per year in costs to the health service and to the economy. Behind those bald numbers, lies untold misery to the sufferers and their family and carers. All of this is inflicted disproportionately on those living in poverty. By taking this one simple action – providing fruit and veg on prescription the government could do so much to assuage that. And now Alexandra Rose Charity has provided the hard evidence, there is no excuse for delay. Their Fruit & Veg on Prescription Project improves not only the diet and health of people but also the health of the local food economy. I urge government to take a look at the impressive results from these pilots and explore how these can be replicated and scaled as part of a ‘Community Eatwell’ approach to tackling food-related ill health in the UK, as recommended in the 2021 National Food Strategy.”
Henry Dimbleby, Author of the National Food Strategy Independent Review
Only 1 in 4 adults eat the recommended five portions of fruit and veg a day. Consequently, in 2019, diets low in fruit and veg accounted for 16,000 premature deaths in the UK. With healthy food more than twice as expensive per calorie than less healthy food, affordability is a huge barrier for people on the lowest incomes to get enough fruit and veg into their diet.
“Food isn’t getting cheaper, healthy food least of all. Our mission is to make it easier for everyone to access fresh fruit and veg in their communities. This is a simple intervention that works. It is now time for the government to act on the evidence and progress to a national roll out of trials of Fruit & Veg and Veg on Prescription as a part of their already stated commitment to the ‘Community Eatwell’ programme. This should form part of wider measures to boost health, address food poverty and reshape our food systems for the health of those most in need.”
Jonathan Pauling, Chief Executive, Alexandra Rose Charity
Run in partnership with the Bromley by Bow Centre in Tower Hamlets and community health practitioners at the AT Beacon Project in Lambeth, almost 200 individuals took part in the project, receiving up to £8 in Rose Vouchers every week, which were spent on the fruit and veg of their choice at local markets and food co-ops.
“We all know that the food we eat plays a vital role in our health, but sadly we are seeing more and more people struggling with food poverty and food-related ill health. At the Beacon Project we understand the importance of building trust in our community in innovative ways to support those who have fallen through the cracks of healthcare systems as a result of inequalities in accessing health and wellbeing support. We know that change is possible, and we see the Fruit & Veg on Prescription project making a significant difference to the health of people in our community.”
Dr Chi Chi Ekhator, GP Lead, AT Beacon Project
With Rose Vouchers covering most or all of their fruit and veg costs, the project also significantly reduces food insecurity, with many people sharing they now worry less about money for food. One participant receiving Rose Vouchers for fruit & veg shared: “Before the Rose Vouchers I didn’t even eat fruit because it takes so much out of my money… but now I don’t have to spend my cash and I can try different fruit and vegetables.”
Funding for the pilots has come from local Public Health teams.
“The Public Health team from Lambeth Council has worked with local providers Alexandra Rose Charity and A.T Beacon to develop and deliver this innovative project. The findings from the pilot are very positive and encouraging. Most importantly, Lambeth residents who have engaged with the project say that the support provided and the opportunity to add fruit and vegetables on prescription to their diet has helped them lead healthier and happier lives.”
Cllr Jim Dickson, Cabinet Member for Healthier Communities
“We are delighted to be collaborating with the Alexandra Rose Charity. This project not only increases access to fruit and veg but also supports local businesses and improves the health and well-being of residents.”
Dr Somen Banerjee, Director of Public Health Tower Hamlets
The full report on the charity’s findings is available to read here:

title: The Importance of Edible Gardens in Urban Areas: Growing Health and Community — Urban Growth
description: Edible gardens are more than just a trend; they are a vital component of urban living. These green spaces provide numerous benefits that enhance the quality of life in cities.
text:
The Importance of Edible Gardens in Urban Areas: Growing Health and Community
Edible gardens are certainly trendy, but they are also a vital component of urban living. These green spaces provide numerous benefits that enhance the quality of life in cities.
We wanted to share why we think edible living gardens are essential:
Connecting with the Earth/ Mother Nature: There's a profound connection that emerges when you nurture a plant from seed to fruition, witnessing the cycle of life firsthand. Tending to a garden, whether it's a small plot or a few potted herbs on a windowsill, fosters a sense of responsibility and appreciation for the natural world. As you care for your plants, you become attuned to the rhythms of the seasons, learning to respect the delicate balance of ecosystems. Harvesting the fruits of your labor not only provides nourishment for your body but also feeds your soul, deepening your connection to the earth and all its wonders.
Health and Nutrition: Gardening encourages the consumption of fresh fruits and vegetables, leading to improved dietary habits and overall health. Having a direct connection to the food we eat promotes better nutrition and wellness, helping to combat urban health issues like obesity and malnutrition.
Environmental Benefits: Of course edible gardens also contribute to urban greening, which improves air quality, reduces the urban heat island effect, and supports biodiversity. These gardens also encourage sustainable practices such as composting and organic gardening, making cities more environmentally friendly.
Community Engagement: A focus we’re particularly interested in — these gardens foster a sense of community by bringing people together around a common goal. They provide opportunities for collaboration, knowledge sharing, and building stronger social networks. Community gardens become hubs of social activity and civic engagement.
Education: Edible gardens serve as living classrooms where people, especially children, can learn about agriculture, ecology, and sustainability. This hands-on experience instills a deeper understanding and appreciation for the environment, teaching valuable life skills. We often work with schools and it’s always a source of joy to see young people discovering where their food comes from!
Economic Benefits: Depending on the size of the garden, growing your own food can reduce grocery bills. Edible gardens can spur urban agriculture businesses, creating jobs related to garden management, maintenance, and produce sales. This boosts the local economy and fosters entrepreneurial spirit.
Mental and Physical Well-being: Gardening is a therapeutic activity that can reduce stress, improve mental health, and provide physical exercise. Spending time outdoors in the garden offers a productive and rewarding way to improve overall well-being.
Resilience and Self-Sufficiency: By growing their own food, urban dwellers can become more self-sufficient and resilient to disruptions in the food supply chain, whether due to economic, environmental, or other crises. This resilience is crucial in an increasingly uncertain world.
Food Security: Edible gardens offer a local source of fresh produce, crucial in urban areas where access to affordable and nutritious food may be limited. By growing fruits and vegetables locally, we can help reduce food deserts and promote food security for all residents, especially in deprived areas of London.
At Urban Growth, we specialise in creating various types of gardens that enhance urban living. From sensory gardens that engage all the senses to community spaces that foster connection, our mission is to transform urban areas into green, sustainable havens. Among these, our edible living gardens stand out as a crucial element, providing a host of benefits to city dwellers. Many of our projects are located in deprived areas of London, making our work particularly important.
Please reach out if you’d like to work with us admin@urbangrowth.london, and follow us on https://instagram.com/urbangrowthlondon for the latest updates and gardening inspiration!

text:
The FRIDGE Project:
A Heartfelt Thank You and Goodbye
After lots of thought and care, we've made the difficult decision to close the FRIDGE project.
The FRIDGE grew from our BOX-IT initiative during the pandemic—a time when food support helped us connect deeply with our community. While BOX-IT responded to a crisis, the FRIDGE was always about creating a space based on trust, respect, and kindness—where people could give and take as they needed, without judgement. It was a community effort built on mutual support—core values of The Bridge.
However, things have changed. New food safety rules, growing demand, and limited space have made it hard to keep the project running in the open, supportive way that we like to work with our community. We've also taken time to reflect on our mission and review how our projects fit. With this in mind, we've realised the FRIDGE is not a project that fully delivers our mission to create kind, welcoming spaces for women to focus on health and wellbeing.
This decision wasn’t easy. We’re incredibly grateful to everyone who’s been part of the FRIDGE—whether you used it, supported it, or helped keep it running. Thank you.
Need support? Postcards with info about local food providers are available at our reception and café.
What’s Next?
We’re working on new projects for women at The Bridge, and we’d love for you to be involved. Keep an eye out for a QR code near the FRIDGE to sign up and stay in the loop.
Got questions?
Email us at projects@thebridge-uk.org or chat with the FRIDGE team when you’re in.
who’s it for?
Everyone.
Whether you are looking for FREE fresh food or want to support others by donating something tasty, the fridge is open for all!
*for information on how to donate food please read section below.
where & when?
The fridge is located in our café at The Bridge, 73–81 Southwark Bridge Road, SE1 0NQ. Find us here.
The fridge is accessible every Thursday between 15:00 - 17:00 and Friday between 09:30 – 14:00.
is there a cost?
No. Access to food items in the fridge are FREE for anyone to take home.
You’re always welcome to support our work in other ways if you can, such as volunteering and/or donating to the Charity.
how does it work?
The Bridge aims to provide accessibility for all. There’s no need to be referred and the fridge will run on a ‘take what you need, leave what you can’ basis to encourage mutual support in the community.
Remember to bring your own bag and help us reduce waste!
To receive updates about the FRIDGE project, please register below. You can unsubscribe anytime.

when is best to access FRIDGE?
The majority of people access FRIDGE between 3:00 PM and 4:00 PM on Thursdays. Although we try our best to ensure a fair share of items for everyone, because of this initial rush, the amount of food available on Fridays is typically lower than it is on Thursdays.
can you provide bags for me to take food home?
Unfortunately we do not have the resources to provide shopping bags. Occasionally bags for life are donated, which we offer (when we can) if someone has no other way of taking items home. If you have unused plastic bags at home please consider bringing them in for us to redistribute!
why can I only queue for FRIDGE from 2:45 PM?
We are committed to making access to FRIDGE as fair as possible. Allowing people to queue too long in advance for FRIDGE excludes those who cannot spare the time to arrive early, and people coming for the first time who may not be aware of how busy we can get on Thursday afternoons.
Our café space also has many functions; large numbers of people waiting for FRIDGE in advance limits others’ ability to enter and exit, and use the community space. For these reasons we begin issuing tickets on a first-come, first-served basis from 2:45 PM.
how do I know what/how much food will be available?
The food accessible through FRIDGE is donated by the Felix Project and local businesses. As these sources are reliant on surplus items, we have no advance warning as to what/how much will be provided, and the selection and quantity varies week by week. Typically, a good amount of bread, sweet baked goods, and some form of fresh produce is delivered every week.
On Wednesday afternoons we aim to send out a list of the items which will be available when we open the following day. This will come via our mailing list, where we also announce closures affecting FRIDGE. Sign up below.
We are working on improving our selection of suppliers to give people access to better quality produce: watch this space!

You don’t need to register to access food from the FRIDGE project, however if you want to receive any updates please fill the form below.
want to donate food?
You can also share surplus food as an individual, e.g. ingredients you’re not going to use in time, things you've grown, if you're going away on holiday or you simply want to support the cause. There are some rules on what you can and cannot put in the fridge (for health and safety reasons) so make sure to check-in with us in advance before you visit.
